summary: This informational RFC is the Statement of Work for extending the IETF Datatracker so that it can provide statistics about RFCs and Internet-Drafts and their authors. It is administrative and describes work to be contracted rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a job description for building a tool that counts things about IETF documents and who wrote them.

subtitle: Tracking who writes IETF standards and where they work

tldr.problem: The IETF community needs better visibility into who is contributing to standards work, which organizations are involved, and how participation is distributed geographically.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC is a Statement of Work for enhancing the IETF Datatracker database with statistical tools to analyze authors, affiliations, and geographic distribution of RFC and Internet-Draft contributors.
tldr.outcome: The resulting tools help the IETF understand community diversity, identify trends in participation, and support decisions about leadership and community engagement.

facts.label: Time period covered
facts.value: Last five years (recent RFCs and Internet-Drafts)

today: RFC 7760 is an Informational RFC published in January 2016. It describes the work scope for a real project: enhancements to the IETF Datatracker to provide author and community statistics. Whether and how completely these enhancements have been implemented is not stated in the RFC itself.

sections.title: Why Count Authors
sections.content: A member of the IETF community created tools to analyze who writes RFCs and Internet-Drafts. These tools examine the documents themselves to gather statistics about authors and their organizations. This RFC describes a plan to move those capabilities into the official IETF Datatracker, so they are maintained as part of the IETF information infrastructure. As much data as possible should come from the Datatracker database rather than being extracted from document text.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone made a tool to count who writes IETF documents. Now the IETF wants to build that into its main database so everyone can use it.

sections.title: What the Statistics Will Show
sections.content: Author statistics help the IETF community see where work happens and by whom. The statistics reveal which individuals, companies, and geographic regions are most active, and show how this changes over the years. Some statistics are informational; others are used to study trends, understand diversity efforts, or identify candidates for leadership roles.
sections.plainLanguage: The statistics show which people are most active, which companies contribute the most, and which countries have the most authors. This helps the IETF see if enough different countries and organizations are involved.

sections.title: What Statistics to Provide
sections.content: The Datatracker should provide statistics and graphs covering: the number of authors per document, document size, the use of specification techniques (ABNF, ASN.1, C code, CBOR, JSON, XML), the distribution of authors by how many documents they have written, the impact of authors measured by citations, affiliations of authors, countries and continents of authors, and countries and continents of IETF meeting attendees. Statistics should cover recent Internet-Drafts, recent RFCs (last five years), and all RFCs. Trends should be shown over time.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool should count authors, their companies, their countries, and which specification techniques each RFC uses. It should show how things change from year to year.

sections.title: How to Build It
sections.content: The existing code can be rewritten with the Datatracker database as the primary source. Some rules and heuristics from the current tool may be useful, such as methods for matching author aliases (since people write their names differently in different documents), recognizing organizations by domain names, and mapping address information to countries and continents. The Datatracker database needs new tables to hold these heuristics, accessible through a web interface for updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The Datatracker needs new tables to remember things like author nicknames, company names, and country codes. These need a web page where people can update them.

sections.title: Rolling It Out
sections.content: The current tools analyze documents directly, so not all needed data is in the Datatracker yet. The development effort will add the capability to capture and store this data for all RFCs and Internet-Drafts from the last five years. It may be cost-effective to leverage the existing code to extract information first, then verify it once before loading it into the Datatracker. The original tools have URLs in many places on the web; the author promises to provide suitable redirects once the Datatracker replacement is available.
sections.plainLanguage: When the new tool is ready, it will be loaded with five years of data. The old website will redirect people to the new one in the Datatracker.
